3. The defence case is that Mir Ali Khandakar, a co-sharer in respect of the disputed Plot No. 6, instituted a partition suit on 4.8.1967 against the father of Afzal Hossain. He obtained a final decree in that suit and got full physical possession through Court by a writ of delivery of possession on 29.9.1980. When Afzal Hossain tried to dispossess him he instituted a suit, being O.C. Suit No. 652 of 1980, for permanent injunction and obtained an order of temporary injunction against Afzal Hossain. In the morning of occurrence Afzal Hossain and P.W. 2 Sarwar Hossain, P.W. 3 Saidur Rahman, P.W. 4 Afzal Hossain, P.W. 5 Fazlul Haque and others came to dispossess Mir Ali Khandakar from the disputed land. Appellants Hamidul Haque, Dulu Mia and Mustafizur Rahman suffered injuries in the hands of complainant party. The deceased Afzal Hossain might have been injured in a melee, but nobody knew who assaulted him. 

 "There is preponderance of oral evidence on record, by P.Ws. 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 that appellant Mir Ali Khandakar never possessed the P.O. land and that the kaun was grown by the deceased Afzal Hossain. He mayor may not have done it in spite of execution of the decree in the partition suit and in spite of an order of temporary injunction, but there is absolutely no oral evidence on record that the accused party was in actual physical possession of the place of land. As such we are of the opinion that no reasonable doubt has been created by the production of the aforesaid defence documents as to manner of occurrence". 

 8. In support of the appellants first contention reliance is also placed on Samiruddin Ahmed @ Samir Mia Vs. The State 1988 BLD (AD) 157. That was a case of criminal trespass. The incident took place on 22.12.1982. In 1978 the accused instituted Title Suit No. 233 of 1978 for permanent injunction in respect of the disputed property and obtained an ad-interim order of injunction on 5.4.1978. The suit was decreed on 19.1.1984 after the trial was over. There was nothing on record to show that the informant party took any step against the order of injunction or that the order was vacated at any time before the alleged date of occurrence. In the background of the case it was held that the Court was required to consider the effect of the order of injunction on the date of the alleged offence. It was further observed that when the decree for permanent injunction was passed it should be taken as a decision as to possession on the date of the institution of the suit. If the appellant was in possession in 1978 as found by the Civil Court then, for the purpose of the criminal case, the prosecution evidence as to possession could not be accepted beyond reasonable doubt. 

 21. The defence case, as clearly made out by cross-examining P.W. 1, the informant, is that appellant Mir Ali, uncle of the deceased, Afzal, had been in possession of the disputed land on the basis of a decree in a Partition Suit followed by Writ of delivery of possession and that when, thereafter, his possession was threatened by Afzal, the latter was restrained by an order of temporary injunction which was in force when the occurrence took place. Though P.W. 1, wife of the deceased, pleaded ignorance about the Civil Court's decree, she at the last stage, accepted the suggestion that an order of injunction was passed against her husband in O.S. No. 652 of 1980. The learned Judges of the High Court Division took note of this evidence but did not accept the defence suggestion that the appellant was in actual physical possession of the land for want of further evidence. Observation of the learned Judges on this particular point is: 

 "He (appellant) mayor may not have done it in spite of execution of the decree in the Partition Suit and in spite of an order of temporary injunction, but there is absolutely no oral evidence on record that the accused party was in actual physical possession of the land." 

 This view as I find, is not in conformity with the established principle of law as to possession of land delivered by a Civil Court's writ, or possession which has been maintained by such Court's injunction, temporary or permanent. If the possession has been delivered by a court in execution of a decree or the possession has otherwise been regulated by an order of injunction, then it must be presumed that the person to whom possession has been delivered or in whose favour order of injunction has been passed is in possession unless evidence is led to the contrary by the person who disputes this possession. This Court, in the case of Samiruddin Ahmed Vs. State, 1988 BLD(AD) 157; (1989) 41 DLR (AD) 129, has observed that an order of injunction presupposes the possession of the person in whose favour the order has been made and that, so long the order of Civil Court is in force, any determination of the question of possession without reference to the order of the Civil Court would be clearly untenable and unacceptable. In the case of Abul Farah Vs. Mozammel Huq, 27 DLR, 260, the High Court Division took the view that if the dispute concerning possession of a land has been finally decided by a Civil Court, the Magistrate's jurisdiction under section 145 Cr. P.C. is ousted. The Pakistan Supreme Court in an authoritative decision in Shah Muhammad Vs. Haq Nawaz; 23 DLR (SC) 14, held: 

 "A case in which a civil court is already seized with the subject-matter of dispute and has passed an order regulating possession thereof or a case in which a decree for possession has been granted or a permanent injunction granted restraining the opposite party from interfering with the possession of the decree-holder, falls outside the jurisdiction of a Magistrate under section 145 Cr.P.C. In such a case if apprehension of breach of peace prevails, the Magistrate can take action under sections 107 and 151 Cr.P.C. and bind down the party threatening to act in violation of the decree of the court or terms of the interim order."
